output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Rania Haddad is an adjunct instructor of academic writing at a university, teaching three sections on a per-course contract with no office, no health insurance, and a paycheck that evaporates by mid-month. She also works as a freelance Arabic-to-English translator, often translating legal documents late into the night, though the income is unpredictable. She lives with her younger brother, his wife, and their toddler in a two-bedroom apartment in Amman, having moved in after her marriage ended two years ago. She contributes what she can from her translation income to the household.

Rania's marriage ended quietly when her independence threatened her ex-husband's authority; she had refused to stop teaching after the wedding, and they separated. She returned to Amman with two suitcases, a few books, and a determination to never again surrender the work that made her feel real. She is warm and attentive, remembering every student who mentioned a sick mother or a broken printer, carrying a mental roster of who needs a quiet word or a copy of lecture notes. She does not lecture about effort but simply shows up with bread and answers. She is patient in explaining but impatient with sloppy thinking, and she listens fully even when pressed for time.

Rania values education as both a door and a discipline, and she values independence and self-sufficiency, prioritizing her work over traditional expectations. She places high value on reciprocal kindness and not being indebted to others. She struggles to accept help, often deflecting kindness and later reciprocating with tangible gifts, sometimes to the confusion of the giver. She keeps a mental ledger of every kindness and answers it with a tangible gift. She also has a habit of bringing bread, jam, or olives to Layla's house at every prior invitation, even when told not to.

Rania also informally tutors students who cannot afford internet, using her kitchen table three evenings a week after dinner, writing on used envelopes and saving paper. Her brother teases her about electricity but makes tea; his wife washes teacups without complaint. At department gatherings, Layla sits beside her and adds extra food to her plate, and Layla's mother treats her like a daughter, calls her 'Auntie' in jest, and sends her home with leftovers. Layla is one of the few colleagues who knows Rania's per-course situation and never presses her about money, often inviting her to family meals.

She has no office or health insurance, and her financial resources are limited. She carries a satchel with marked essays and a dish towel with leftovers.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Rania's friend Layla, a fellow adjunct from the English department, invites her to a small family dinner this Friday. Layla says on the phone, "Please, don't bring anything. I know you're busy, and you have enough to carry. Just come and spend time." Rania knows that in Jordanian custom, showing up empty-handed to a meal feels rude, even though Layla is also Jordanian and knows the custom herself. Rania has a jar of apricot jam she made and a fresh loaf of bread at home. She could bring them anyway, explaining it's a small token of appreciation, or she could respect Layla's request and arrive without anything, trusting that her presence is enough.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Rania has been up late translating a lease agreement for two nights and is running on less sleep than usual. This morning she baked a fresh loaf and sealed a new batch of apricot jam, and the kitchen still smells of warm bread. She is looking forward to a quiet evening after a heavy week of marking, though she also knows her pantry is nearly empty.

Layla's phrase "don't bring anything" reminds Rania of last spring, when she brought a loaf anyway and Layla's mother exclaimed that it was better than the bakery's. The sight of the jam jar on the counter recalls the summer she and Layla made jam together after Layla's father's funeral, working side by side in silence.
